claims.text: Explicitly decoupling lattice and electronic thermal conductivity will produce more accurate channel-specific predictions for HfNbTaTiZr.
The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity over 300–1200 K.
Electronic thermal conductivity becomes dominant below 200 K.
The new model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20% relative to models that conflate lattice and electronic transport.
The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr that is defect-free or nearly defect-free.
A sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen is representative of the controlled-impurity condition for high-temperature validation.
The approach separately analyzes phonon and electronic transport using atomistic simulation, electronic-structure information, and analytical transport calculations.
The high-temperature regime from 300 to 1200 K has a stronger lattice contribution than the low-temperature regime.
Atomic-mass variation and the distribution of force constants mediate thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic-structure calculations provide the microscopic information needed to model the electronic thermal-transport channel.
Separately fitting lattice and electronic channels to their temperature dependencies avoids averaging errors associated with conflated approaches.
Temperature-dependent parameter adaptation captures the relevant scattering mechanisms.
High-temperature lattice thermal conductivity will be approximately 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier analytical and simulation approaches either assume perfect crystals or conflate lattice and electronic heat conduction.
Earlier approaches deviate from experiment by more than 20% when impurity and temperature effects are non-negligible.
The model is applicable only from approximately 100 to 1200 K under thermodynamic equilibrium.
Heavily defected HfNbTaTiZr may invalidate the model assumptions.
A prediction error exceeding 20% across the tested temperature range would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the electronic contribution to dominate below 200 K would falsify the hypothesis.
A significant discrepancy between predicted and measured high-temperature lattice conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis emphasizes separation of lattice and electronic transport, but the predicted high-temperature lattice value of 10–17 W/(K m) is taken from a total-conductivity measurement. This reassigns a total value to one channel and therefore conflates the quantities the model is supposed to separate.

The sample is described as defect-free while also allowing 1 wt.% oxygen. Unless oxygen is explicitly represented as a homogeneous substitutional component, that impurity level introduces chemical disorder or point defects inconsistent with a strictly defect-free sample.
